brief.title: How a browser decides to reuse a response
brief.idea: The server, not the browser, decides when a stored copy may be reused: fresh means no request at all, stale means a tiny fingerprint check, and changing the file's name is how you ship a fix.
brief.gap: The viewer sees cache headers like max-age, no-cache and ETag but cannot say what the browser actually does with them, or why a fix they shipped does not reach users.
brief.for: web developers who ship sites but have never reasoned through HTTP caching

case.text: A small shop site with three files: logo.png changes once a year, app.js changes every deploy, and the /cart response is different for each user.

material.text: Each page load asks for dozens of files (HTML, CSS, scripts, images, fonts), and most have not changed since the last visit.
A cache is a local store of earlier responses; the browser looks there before it sends a request.
The question the browser must answer for each file: use my stored copy, or ask the server?
The server sets the rules, not the browser, as response headers sent with each file.
Cache-Control: max-age=N marks the copy fresh for N seconds; while fresh, the browser uses it without contacting the server at all. Zero network, the fastest outcome.
A copy older than max-age is stale. Stale does not mean wrong; it means the browser must check before using it.
That check is revalidation. The server gave the file a fingerprint, the ETag header (a short string that changes when the content changes); the browser sends it back in If-None-Match.
If the fingerprint still matches, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, a few hundred bytes instead of the whole file; the browser keeps its copy and the freshness clock restarts.
If the fingerprint does not match, the server answers 200 with the new file and a new ETag.
Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since is the older form of the same check, using a date; dates have one-second resolution, which is why ETag is preferred.
Every request ends one of three ways: fresh hit (no request), revalidated (small request, 304), or miss (full download).
no-cache does not mean do not cache: it means store it, but revalidate every time before using it. The name misleads almost everyone.
no-store means keep no copy at all; use it for private data such as a bank statement.
The hard problem: with a long max-age, users keep the old file until it expires, and you cannot reach into their cache to ship a fix.

The standard answer is to change the URL when the content changes: build tools put a content hash in the file name (app.3f9a1c.js), so a new build is a new cache entry and the old one is never asked for again.
Hashed files can be cached for good: Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable (one year; immutable tells the browser not to revalidate even on reload).
The HTML page that points at hashed files must stay revalidated (no-cache), or users never learn the new file names.
The common recipe: HTML no-cache; hashed assets one year, immutable; API responses with private data no-store or private.
private means only the user's own browser may store the response; shared caches such as a CDN must not. public allows shared caches.
A CDN is a shared cache between many users and the server, following the same rules and headers; s-maxage sets a freshness time for shared caches only.
Rule of thumb: the cheapest request is the one that is never sent.

chapters.question: What will you understand by the end?

beats.says: In the next five minutes, you'll see how a browser decides to reuse a file it already has, and why a fix you ship sometimes never reaches your users.
This is HTTP caching. The browser keeps the files, but the server writes the rules for reusing them.

chapters.question: Who decides whether a stored copy can be reused?

beats.says: So when the browser already has a file, who decides whether it can reuse it?
A cache is a local store of earlier responses. Before any request goes out, the browser looks there and asks: can I use my stored copy, or must I ask the server?

frames.shows: A pipeline left to right: the browser, its cache box in the middle, the server on the right, and a question callout above the cache.

a question callout over the cache

cues.does: draws its outline and fills in the middle
pops in on the left and a line grows from it into the cache
types on above the cache
draws itself on the right, a dashed line reaching it

beats.says: Take a small shop site. Its logo changes once a year. Its script, app dot js, changes every deploy. And its cart page is different for every shopper.

pops in under the logo

beats.says: Each visit, the browser asks for those files and dozens more, and most haven't changed since last time.

cues.does: glows as a request line runs to the cache
appears tile by tile behind the three chips
most tiles change to good, marked unchanged

beats.says: The answer isn't the browser's to make. The server decides, and sends its rules as response headers on every file.

cues.does: dims
changes from dim to active and glows

beats.says: This means that to understand caching, you read the headers.

chapters.question: How long can a copy be reused without asking the server?

beats.says: Let's start with the first rule, which is about time.
A header called Cache-Control can carry max-age, a number of seconds. For that long the copy is fresh, and the browser uses it without contacting the server at all.

frames.shows: A header line at the top, a freshness bar under it, the browser with its cache on the left and a dim server on the right with a cross on the line between them.

objects.what: a header set as a code line
a freshness bar labelled in seconds
a cross on the line to the server

cues.does: types on at the top
appears empty under the header
fills to full and turns good
glows as the copy comes out of the cache
pops onto the line to the dim server

beats.says: That means zero network. No request, no waiting. It's the fastest outcome there is.
Say the shop's logo arrives with a max-age of one day. All that day, every page shows it straight from the cache.

frames.shows: The shop's logo in the cache with its header, a one-day freshness bar, and a row of page icons each drawing the logo from the cache.

its header as a code line
a freshness bar for one day
a row of page icons, each with a short line from the cache

cues.does: pops into the cache
types on beside the logo as the bar under it fills
page icons pop in one after another, a line to the cache for each
glows

beats.says: Once the day is up, the copy is stale. Stale doesn't mean wrong. It means the browser must check before using it.

objects.what: a pill on the logo chip
a callout with an arrow toward a server off to the right

cues.does: runs down to empty and turns dim
pops onto the logo, which stays plain, not crossed
types on with an arrow growing toward the server

beats.says: But checking doesn't mean downloading again.

chapters.question: How does the browser check a stale copy without downloading it?

beats.says: That check is called revalidation. When the server first sent the file, it gave it a fingerprint: the ETag, a short string that changes whenever the content does.

frames.shows: Two lifelines, the browser on the left and the server on the right, under a title; the first response has crossed from server to browser carrying the file with a fingerprint tag.

cues.does: types on at the top

pops onto the file as a tag

beats.says: To revalidate, the browser sends that fingerprint back in a header called If-None-Match. Is this still the one?

cues.does: travels from the browser lifeline to the server
glows at the server, the tag on the file ringed with it

beats.says: If it matches, the server answers three-oh-four, Not Modified, with no body. A few hundred bytes instead of the whole file. The browser keeps its copy, and the freshness clock starts again.

beats.says: If it doesn't match, the server answers two hundred, with the new file and a new fingerprint.

beats.says: So the shop's logo, a day old, costs one tiny three-oh-four, and another day of free reuse.

cues.does: pops onto the file as the 200 branch dims

beats.says: You'll also meet an older check, Last-Modified, which uses a date instead. Dates only count whole seconds, so the fingerprint wins.

frames.shows: Two comparison cards side by side: ETag with a fingerprint on the left marked preferred, Last-Modified with a date on the right, dimmed, with a note about one-second resolution under it.

objects.what: verdict pill on the left card

cues.does: pops in on the right, facing the ETag card on the left

beats.says: So now we have all three outcomes: a fresh hit, a revalidation, or a full download.

chapters.question: If a copy stays fresh for long, how do you ship a fix?

beats.says: Now the hard part. A long max-age is fast, but users keep the old file until it expires, and you can't reach into their cache.

beats.says: Say the shop ships a bug fix in app dot js. Anyone holding last week's copy keeps running the bug.

cues.does: pops in at the server
glows in the cache
pops onto the old copy, which turns bad

beats.says: But there's a way out, and it isn't waiting.
The standard answer: change the address when the content changes. Build tools put a content hash in the file name, like app dot three f nine a one c dot js.

beats.says: A new build means a new name, so a new cache entry. The old one is simply never asked for again.

a cache box on the far right

cues.does: comes out of the build under the first name

beats.says: So cache hashed files for good. Give them a max-age of one year, plus immutable, which tells the browser not to revalidate even on reload.

beats.says: But the HTML page that names those files can't be cached like that. It must be revalidated, or users never learn the new names.

chapters.question: Which header goes on which of the shop's files?

beats.says: That's how a fix gets through. Now let's put a header on each of the shop's files.
Give the HTML no-cache. And don't trust the name: no-cache doesn't mean don't store it. It means store it, but revalidate before every use.

frames.shows: A stack of rows, one per shop file; only the first is there: HTML, no-cache, with a crossed-out misreading and the true meaning beside it.

objects.what: a crossed-out keyword beside the row

cues.does: pops in at the top of the stack

beats.says: App dot js, with its hashed name, gets one year and immutable. Give the logo a hashed name and it can have the same.

cues.does: dims as the next row pops in under it
pops in as the second row
pops in as the third row

beats.says: The cart is private data. Give it no-store, which keeps no copy at all, or private, which lets only the shopper's own browser keep one.

beats.says: Private matters because of shared caches, like a CDN between many users and your server. Public lets a CDN store a response, and s-maxage sets a freshness time for shared caches only.

beats.says: Under all of it sits one rule: the cheapest request is the one that's never sent.

chapters.question: So what does the browser decide on the shop's next visit?

beats.says: So a browser never guesses. Fresh means no request, stale means a tiny check, and a new name is how your fix gets through.

frames.shows: Three chips in a row: fresh means no request, stale means a 304 check, a new name means the fix ships.

cues.does: pops in on the left
pops in beside it
pops in on the right and glows

beats.says: Open your own site's network panel, look at the headers on each file, and tell me in the comments which one surprised you.
Thanks for watching. See you next time.
